nodes.title: Train small reference models on HPLT 4.0 clean data
Determine "hard cut-offs" for data using propella annotations
Agree with pretraining team on the context extension parameters
nodes.description:
Highlevel, this task comes to optimizing the full pipeline on the models we want to deliver and the expectations on those models. 
Between the pre- and post-training, we need to agree on optimization of the long context capability.

Key questions to anwer:
**1. what is the amount of compute / data we should use for the context extension?**

The amount of compute is decisive factor on deciding what options we have for context extension.

We can roughly classify the ways to do context extension as follows:

* Pretraining type of training: Continue with pretraining objective, but use longer sequence length data and training than during pretraining. Also some synthetic data may be added to the training dataset here
* RoPE (Rotary position embedding) scaling related training: We use longer sequence length in addition to RoPE scaling to teach the model long context relationships. This does not require that long training, but in practice often does not work as well as 1.
* Hybrid/combination of the above, where type 1 training is first used and it is further extended with type 2 training.

There are also some architecture related matters that matter here as the attention calculation operation is exponential in compute relative to sequence length, so the longer sequence lengths are always more expensive. Some new architectural choices like use of linear attention matter and they may be negligible in cost on pretraining but matter in context extension / post training. Also long context performance  may be optimal with different kind of model than with shorter sequence model performance. One new paper regarding this https://allenai.org/papers/olmpool

**2. which parameters are used in pretraining, and what is adequate for long context purposes?**

There are other parameters like RoPE base frequency (AKA RoPE Theta) that needs some discussion. Pretraining has done most of the experiments using RoPE base of 10000 which is quite small for long context purposes and this should be probably changed in some part of training.

nodes.title: Preliminary English function-calling SFT dataset for OpenEuroLLM
nodes.description:
## Status — dataset preparation delivered

The selected function-calling corpus and native OELLM 64K preparation are complete. The active verl work is turning that prepared corpus into a trained, exported and evaluated OELLM checkpoint; those downstream outcomes are separate from this dataset-preparation deliverable.

Dataset location: [openeurollm/function-calling-sft-oellm-64k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openeurollm/function-calling-sft-oellm-64k).

## Delivered

- Published selection and reproducible export code in [fcanalysis](https://github.com/lightonai/fcanalysis): nine datasets through eleven exports, with pinned sources, explicit exclusions, preserved reasoning and completion reports. See the [selection and export recipe](https://github.com/lightonai/fcanalysis/blob/89fb5f31f7935dc761233fcd15000931224a85bb/docs/loading.md#export-retained-conversations) and [export script](https://github.com/lightonai/fcanalysis/blob/89fb5f31f7935dc761233fcd15000931224a85bb/scripts/export_selected_source.py).
- Materialized canonical exports: **2,564,952 conversations before cross-source deduplication; 2,547,674 afterward**, with Terminal handled separately from native function-call data.
- Complete native OELLM preparation: tokenizer/template rendering, assistant-token supervision, compatible target grouping, fixed holdout, **65,536-token admission**, exclusion accounting and training Parquet files. The completed data is staged for training.

Publication of the selection/code and availability of the prepared dataset do not establish clearance of all underlying training, redistribution or publication rights. Source-specific rights decisions remain tracked in #390.

## Current native OELLM accounting

| Measure | Training | Holdout |
|---|---:|---:|
| Assigned conversations | 2,542,659 | 5,015 |
| Prepared rows | 8,408,269 | 16,796 |
| Admitted assistant targets | 12,341,492 | 24,818 |
| Input tokens | 41,342,243,905 | 81,841,598 |
| Supervised tokens | 7,024,161,274 | 14,178,527 |

Rows and targets differ because compatible targets can share a row. The training partition includes **158 conversations with no admitted target**. The context limit covers masked context plus supervised assistant output; over-limit targets are excluded without truncation, while other fitting targets in the same conversation remain eligible.

These figures come from the validated selected-accounting report for the completed preparation. Token counts depend on the checkpoint tokenizer/template, target grouping and loss masks; they are distinct from the canonical export script's conversation and assistant-message counts.

## Changes from the September 14 snapshot

- **Selection:** APIGen-MT and the specified separable APIGen derivatives are excluded; Nemotron-Terminal is included. The linked export recipe defines the exact current subsets and exclusions.
- **Model:** the current starting checkpoint is [Neonkraft/oellm-9b-256k-theta64m-prelude-anneal300b-instruct-sft](https://huggingface.co/Neonkraft/oellm-9b-256k-theta64m-prelude-anneal300b-instruct-sft), revision `85bf18fb4f0bee6ac6270f06b1d1c6b3be200f31`. It uses a dense Qwen3 architecture and its native tokenizer/template. Earlier Qwen3.5 token counts and backend assumptions do not transfer.
- **Context:** this preparation and run use 64K admission, despite the checkpoint's advertised 256K capacity.
- **Comparison:** the untouched OELLM starting checkpoint already underwent prior SFT; it is the baseline for the current function-calling run.

The earlier **2,349,507 conversations, 10,426,741 admitted samples and 4.407B supervised tokens**, together with the old per-source tables, grouping reductions, token-category percentages and exclusion counts, are historical measurements of a different corpus/rendering configuration.

## Follow-up responsibilities

| Issue | Status | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| #385 — Train and export the OELLM 9B function-calling SFT checkpoint on LUMI | Open | Complete full selected-mixture training, checkpoint continuation and final HF export verification; hand off the usable checkpoint and matching baseline/evaluation protocol. |
| #384 — Qwen3.5 BFCL V4 non-Web comparison | Completed | Base and post-trained Qwen3.5 results are recorded. OELLM before/after evaluation will be tracked in a separate follow-up after #385, using its native tokenizer/template/parser and explicitly stated category coverage. |
| #386 — Agentic RL stack on LUMI | Open | Downstream environment/rollout/reward/update/checkpoint integration after useful SFT results; outside the completed dataset-preparation scope. |
| #390 — Licensing and mixture ablations | Open | Resolve source-specific training, redistribution and publication rights; revise the mixture and recount if needed. Controlled mixture ablations remain separate from preparation completion. |
| #387 — Deduplication research | Closed as not planned | Additional seed-family selection and weighting research is not currently planned. |
| #388 — Scale agentic/RL data generation | Closed as not planned | Dedicated scaling work is not currently planned. |
| #389 — Multilingual function-calling data generation | Closed as not planned | A dedicated multilingual generation pipeline is not currently planned. |

Full training, final exported-tensor verification and before/after capability evaluation remain unfinished. Their execution status belongs in the downstream issues rather than this dataset-preparation record.

<details>
<summary>Historical September 14 corpus and rendering snapshot</summary>

## Audited baseline — 2026-09-14

Historical **greeting-retaining** full-corpus census from September 14. These figures describe the earlier corpus/rendering configuration and are superseded by the current OELLM accounting above. The incomplete greeting-free recount was excluded.

| Coverage | Count |
|---|---:|
| Source conversations before global deduplication | 2,371,316 |
| Retained conversations after global deduplication | 2,349,507 |
| Original assistant targets | 10,567,468 |
| Admitted reference training samples | 10,426,741 |
| Targets excluded above 65,536 tokens | 137,734 |
| Unrenderable opening greetings | 2,417 |
| Other rendering exclusions | 576 |
| Conversations with no admitted target | 147 |

The 2,417 unrenderable greetings did not remove their conversations; 16,152 later targets from those conversations are admitted.

## Training layouts

All layouts supervise every admitted target exactly once.

| Layout | Samples | Processed tokens | Masked tokens | Trainable tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Per-assistant reference | 10,426,741 | 42,171,055,528 | 37,763,767,782 | 4,407,287,746 |
| Partial grouping, K=2 | 7,702,946 | 31,232,523,796 | 26,825,236,050 | 4,407,287,746 |
| Maximal compatible grouping | 6,466,509 | 23,903,683,294 | 19,496,395,548 | 4,407,287,746 |

K=2 reduces processed-token work by 25.94%; maximal grouping reduces it by 43.32%. These are token-work reductions, not measured training-speed gains. Processed tokens include repeated conditioning prefixes and exclude padding and packing overhead.

| Trainable category | Tokens | Share |
|---|---:|---:|
| Assistant reasoning | 1,660,807,635 | 37.68% |
| Assistant visible prose | 2,217,840,921 | 50.32% |
| Serialized tool calls | 485,749,978 | 11.02% |
| Target formatting/control | 42,889,212 | 0.97% |
| **Total** | **4,407,287,746** | **100%** |

Tool-call tokens include serialized structure, names, and arguments. Tool results are masked context. In the reference layout, 10.45% of processed tokens are trainable and 89.55% are masked.

## Dataset distribution

Counts are after global deduplication and length/rendering admission. Token columns are millions, rounded; native subsets are combined.

| Dataset family | Conversations | Samples | Processed M | Masked M | Trainable M |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| APIGen-MT | 4,306 | 37,897 | 207.294 | 203.779 | 3.515 |
| Dolci | 199,011 | 1,046,056 | 1,868.766 | 1,777.535 | 91.231 |
| Nemotron v1 | 181,275 | 654,459 | 1,982.220 | 1,516.176 | 466.044 |
| Nemotron v2 | 695,996 | 3,403,440 | 15,562.171 | 14,009.176 | 1,552.994 |
| Toucan | 918,222 | 3,842,881 | 14,039.770 | 12,474.649 | 1,565.121 |
| TxT360 (all three subsets) | 292,875 | 1,035,798 | 2,496.059 | 1,871.005 | 625.054 |
| ToolMind | 23,614 | 31,102 | 50.150 | 32.148 | 18.002 |
| ToolMind Web QA | 4,459 | 152,319 | 4,413.479 | 4,365.742 | 47.737 |
| UltraData | 29,749 | 222,789 | 1,551.146 | 1,513.557 | 37.589 |

## Accounting boundaries

- The 65,536-token limit covers the complete sample: masked context plus trainable assistant output. Over-limit targets are excluded without truncation; other targets in the same conversation remain eligible.
- Before length admission, renderable candidates contain 59,324,609,947 processed and 4,455,845,135 trainable tokens. Length admission removes 17,153,554,419 processed and 48,557,389 trainable tokens.
- Unrenderable targets have unknown token lengths and are not counted as zero.
- The masked-token total is not yet decomposed by system, user, tool results, or historical assistant content. Reasoning removed by a native template is absent from both masked and trainable counts.
- The 4,096-token benchmarking generation cap is separate from SFT admission.

</details>

### Goal

Close the gap between our current throughput and reference implementation numbers on 256 GPUs:

| Reference | Precision | Target TFLOPs/s/GPU |
|---|---|---|
| [Megatron-MoE-ModelZoo](https://github.com/yanring/Megatron-MoE-ModelZoo/tree/main/best_practice/qwen3#performance-results) | BF16 | 276 |
| [Megatron Bridge / NeMo](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/performance-summary.html#model-qwen3-235b-a22b) | FP8 | 238 |
| **Current (Jupiter, GH200 @ 680W)** | **FP8** | **170–175** |

Note: reference numbers are on non-power-capped hardware (H100). The ~60–100 TFLOPs gap is partially attributable to the 680W power cap on Jupiter GH200s (vs 900W rated), but there is likely additional headroom to recover through config tuning.

---

### System

[Jupiter](https://www.fz-juelich.de/en/ias/jsc/systems/supercomputers/jupiter) — NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, 96 GB HBM3, Quad-rail NDR200 InfiniBand

nodes.description:
# Jupiter vs. Snellius GPU Diagnostics

**Date:** 2026-04-02  
**Purpose:** Investigate why Jupiter (GH200) is slower than Snellius (H100) for MoE pretraining.


TL;DR: Jupiter has the GH200 powercapped to 680 from the TDP of 900W. This constraints compute in TFLOPs, resulting in lower throughput compared to Snellius H100.
https://wandb.ai/openeurollm-project/jupiter-snellius-gpt-oss-20b


**Systems under test:**
- **Jupiter** — `jpbo-*` nodes, NVIDIA GH200 96GB HBM3
- **Snellius** — `gcn*` nodes, NVIDIA H100 94GB HBME2e

---

## 1. Tensor Core Throughput (dcgmproftester, Test 1004)

Tensor Activity operation throughput measured with `dcgmproftester13 --no-dcgm-validation -t 1004`.

### Jupiter — Compute node `jpbo-057-39` (4 GPUs)

```
Worker 0:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 5.40e+05 gflops
Worker 1:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 5.41e+05 gflops
Worker 2:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 5.35–5.42e+05 gflops
Worker 3:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 5.30e+05 gflops
```

**~530–540 GFLOPS/GPU**

### Jupiter — Login node `jpbl-s02-03` (1 GPU, no power cap)

```
Worker 0:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 7.17–7.23e+05 gflops
```

**~718–723 GFLOPS/GPU**

### Snellius — `gcn157` (4 GPUs)

```
Worker 0:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 6.85e+05 gflops
Worker 1:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 6.70e+05 gflops
Worker 2:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 6.60–6.72e+05 gflops
Worker 3:0 [1004]: TensorEngineActive: 6.67e+05 gflops
```

**~660–685 GFLOPS/GPU**

### Summary

| System | Node type | TFLOPS/GPU |
|---|---|---|
| Jupiter GH200 | Compute node (power capped) | ~530–540 |
| Jupiter GH200 | Login node (no cap) | ~718–723 |
| Snellius H100 | Compute node | ~660–685 |

> **Finding:** Jupiter compute nodes achieve only ~530 TFLOPS vs. ~720 TFLOPS on the uncapped login node and ~670 TFLOPS on Snellius. This points to aggressive power capping on the compute nodes.

---

## 2. GPU Hardware Specs

Extracted from `dcgmproftester` device output.

| Property | Jupiter GH200 | Snellius H100 |
|---|---|---|
| Compute Capability | 9.0 | 9.0 |
| Multiprocessors | 132 | 132 |
| Shared Memory/SM | 228 KB | 228 KB |
| Memory Bus Width | **6144-bit** | 6016-bit |
| Memory Clock Rate | **2619 MHz** | 1593 MHz |
| **Max Memory Bandwidth** | **4022.8 GB/s** | **2395.9 GB/s** |
| ECC | Enabled | Enabled |

> **Note:** GH200 has significantly higher theoretical memory bandwidth (4 TB/s vs 2.4 TB/s) due to the HBM3e + NVLink-C2C architecture, but this advantage is not materializing in practice due to power constraints.

---

## 3. Power Draw

### During dcgmproftester (compute benchmark) queried with

#### Jupiter — Login node (1 GPU)

```
power.draw.average [W], power.draw.instant [W], module.power.draw.average [W], module.power.draw.instant [W]
power.draw [W], power.draw.instant [W]
793.39 W, 777.70 W, 945.77 W, 917.04 W
795.09 W, 724.22 W, 947.90 W, 851.82 W
784.58 W, 712.76 W, 937.75 W, 849.36 W
792.47 W, 836.97 W, 944.27 W, 951.55 W
```

**~800W** GPU H200
**~150W** Grace and memory
**~950W** GH200 module (total)

#### Jupiter — Compute node `jpbo-039-20` (4 GPUs)
GH200 module has shared power consumption for GPU, Grace CPU and memory
To query:
```
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=power.draw.average,power.draw.instant,module.power.draw.average,module.power.draw.instant   --format=csv, --loop=1
```

```
power.draw.average [W], power.draw.instant [W], module.power.draw.average [W], module.power.draw.instant [W]
526.46 W, 527.90 W, 634.24 W, 637.60 W
527.42 W, 517.71 W, 624.10 W, 608.82 W
513.89 W, 522.82 W, 629.51 W, 639.00 W
529.50 W, 535.04 W, 633.07 W, 638.16 W
```

**~530W** GPU H200
**~100W** Grace and memory
**~630W** GH200 module (total)

#### Snellius — `gcn157` (4 GPUs)

```
power.draw [W], power.draw.instant [W]
690.37 W, 695.87 W
687.66 W, 699.21 W
691.61 W, 696.69 W
```

**~690W** GPU H100

> **Finding:** Jupiter compute nodes are **hard-capped at 680W** (vs. 900W max). Critically, on GH200 this budget is **shared** across the Grace CPU, HBM memory subsystem, and the GPU, so the GPU itself will only draw max 530W as the rest of the module additionally draws more than 100W. This directly explains the ~25% throughput gap in tensor operations vs. the uncapped login node.

---

## 4. Single-Node NCCL `all_reduce` Bandwidth

**Config:** 4 GPUs × 1 node, `minBytes=4B → maxBytes=8GB`, 20 iterations.

### Jupiter — `jpbo-072-01` (4× GH200)

```
# Using devices
#  Rank 0–3 on jpbo-072-01: NVIDIA GH200 120GB

# Out of bounds values : 0 OK
# Avg bus bandwidth    : 119.465 GB/s

# Large message peak (8 GB):
  8589934592   2147483648   float   sum   38261.2 us   224.51 GB/s   336.76 GB/s
```

### Snellius — `gcn82` (4× H100)

```
# Using devices
#  Rank 0–3 on gcn82: NVIDIA H100

# Out of bounds values : 0 OK
# Avg bus bandwidth    : 118.02 GB/s

# Large message peak (8 GB):
  8589934592   2147483648   float   sum   38431 us   223.52 GB/s   335.28 GB/s
```

### Summary

| System | Avg Bus BW | Peak Bus BW (8 GB) |
|---|---|---|
| Jupiter GH200 | 119.5 GB/s | 336.8 GB/s |
| Snellius H100 | 118.0 GB/s | 335.3 GB/s |

> **Finding:** Intra-node collective bandwidth is **essentially identical** between the two systems. NVLink is not a bottleneck.

---

## 5. Two-Node NCCL `all_reduce` Bandwidth

**Config:** 8 GPUs across 2 nodes on the same switch, `minBytes=4B → maxBytes=8GB`.

### Jupiter — `jpbo-028-47` + `jpbo-028-48` (2× 4× GH200)

```
# Out of bounds values : 0 OK
# Avg bus bandwidth    : 49.35 GB/s

# Large message peak (8 GB):
  8589934592   2147483648   float   sum   94268.3 us   91.12 GB/s   159.46 GB/s
```

### Snellius — `gcn73` + `gcn76` (2× 4× H100)

```
# Out of bounds values : 0 OK
# Avg bus bandwidth    : 47.42 GB/s

# Large message peak (8 GB):
  8589934592   2147483648   float   sum   96146 us   89.34 GB/s   156.35 GB/s
```

### Summary

| System | Avg Bus BW | Peak Bus BW (8 GB) |
|---|---|---|
| Jupiter GH200 | 49.35 GB/s | 159.5 GB/s |
| Snellius H100 | 47.42 GB/s | 156.4 GB/s |

> **Finding:** Cross-node collective bandwidth is comparable and Jupiter is marginally ahead. Inter-node networking is **not** a bottleneck.

---

## 6. Pretraining Throughput — GPT-OSS 20B (Single Node)
Result and config can be found here: https://wandb.ai/openeurollm-project/jupiter-snellius-gpt-oss-20b

**Config:** `gbs=16`, `mbs=1`, single node (4 GPUs).

| System | Observed (TFLOP/s/GPU) | Peak (TFLOP/s/GPU, BF16) | Max Achieved (TFLOP/s/GPU) | MFU | MFU powercapped | Power Cap | Throughput (TFLOP/s) | Throughput (tok/s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Snellius H100 | 275 | 989 | 685 | 27.8% | 38% | 700W | 6.70e+05 | 34.5k |
| Jupiter GH200 | 246 | 989 | 540 | 25.5% | 47% | 680W | 5.40e+05 | 31k |

> **Finding:** Jupiter is ~11% behind Snellius in MFU for Qwen. Given identical NCCL performance, this gap is attributable to reduced per-GPU compute throughput from the power cap.

---

nodes.title: Investigating Multilingual Post-Training Data Performance
nodes.description:
## Overview

We're investigating how to add multilingual capabilities to OLMo-3-7B without catastrophic forgetting of English. Starting from our reproduced instruct SFT checkpoint, we continue training on mixtures of English + EU-language data at varying ratios.

### Background: Dolci-Instruct-SFT is 93% English

The base checkpoint's training data (2.15M samples) is overwhelmingly English with a long tail of ~160 languages, each below ~0.4% (Spanish is 2nd largest with ~0.39% (instruct) ~0.41% (think)).

Count-based:
![Dolci-Instruct-SFT language counts](https://github.com/ferreirafabio/open-instruct/blob/main/oellm/experiments/dolci_distribution/results/dolci_language_counts.png?raw=true)

Percentage-based (w.r.t. the respective dataset):
![Dolci-Instruct-SFT language percentage](https://github.com/ferreirafabio/open-instruct/blob/main/oellm/experiments/dolci_distribution/results/dolci_language_distribution.png?raw=true)

### Setup

| | |
|---|---|
| **Base checkpoint** | OLMo-3-7B-Instruct-SFT (reproduced, [details](https://github.com/allenai/open-instruct/issues/1352#issuecomment-2823953936)) |
| **Judge (Elo)** | Qwen3.5-27B (dense, via vllm serve, both orderings, 8k max tokens) |
| **Judge (winrate)** | Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (VLLM, both orderings, 8k max tokens) |
| **Elo benchmark** | LMArena, Bradley-Terry, 100 bootstraps, 200 battles/language, 12 EU languages |
| **Winrate benchmarks** | m-arena-hard-EU (6000 prompts, 12 EU languages), arena-hard (500 English prompts) |
| **Training languages** | en + de, es, fr, it, pt, pl, nl, cs (ratio varies by experiment) |
| **Eval languages** | en, de, es, fr, it, pt, pl, nl, cs, ro, el, uk (12 languages available in LMArena) |
| **Held-out languages** | ro, el (zero-shot transfer test, not in training data) |

### Experiment tracks

| Track | Question | Design |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Preliminary: does the English/EU ratio matter? | 90/80/70% English, ~95k samples, fusion-synth only, EU share split equally across 8 languages |
| **B** | Does more diverse data help? | Same ratios, ~490k samples, fusion-synth + wildchat, lmsys-chat, oasst2 |
| **C** | Is English regression caused by EU data, or by continued SFT itself? | 100% English control (no EU data), same total samples |
| **D** | Does replaying the base checkpoint's English data reduce forgetting? | Same ratios as Track A, but English from Dolci-Instruct-SFT (base checkpoint's own training data) |
| **E** | Does Dolci replay scale with more data? | Same as Track D, but ~490k samples instead of ~95k |

### Full experiment matrix

| Exp. | En/EU | N | Elo | Elo en | Elo w/o en | EU WR% | en WR% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** | — | — | 741±9 | **950±21** | 722±10 | 50% | 50% |
| **A1-90en** | 90/10 | 94.7k | 702±10 | 771±32 | 692±10 | **54.8%** | 14.1% |
| **A2-80en** | 80/20 | 93.6k | 704±11 | 769±30 | 703±11 | **57.2%** | 12.4% |
| **A3-70en** | 70/30 | 91.7k | 713±10 | 766±29 | 689±11 | **58.8%** | 13.3% |
| **B1-90en** | 90/10 | 491k | 720±9 | 789±26 | 708±10 | 53.6% | 13.0% |
| **B2-80en** | 80/20 | 473k | 722±9 | 797±26 | 722±10 | 52.9% | 14.2% |
| **C0-100en** | 100/0 | 94.7k | 670±11 | 791±29 | 681±11 | 48.9% | 11.8% |
| **D1-90en** | 90/10 | 94.7k | **751±8** | **942±20** | 716±11 | **63.4%** | **54.6%** |
| **D2-80en** | 80/20 | 93.6k | **751±8** | **956±20** | **725±12** | **62.0%** | **54.6%** |
| **D3-70en** | 70/30 | 91.7k | **753±9** | **963±21** | **731±11** | **63.5%** | **54.3%** |
| **E1-90en** | 90/10 | 491k | **758±9** | **965±21** | **740±9** | **59.9%** | **57.0%** |
| **E2-80en** | 80/20 | 474k | **759±8** | **931±24** | **725±9** | **56.6%** | **58.2%** |
| **E3-70en** | 70/30 | 455k | **751±9** | **940±22** | **726±9** | 53.1% | **58.6%** |

Elo: Qwen3.5-27B judge. "en" = English-only (200 battles). "w/o en" = 11 non-English languages.

EU WR% / en WR% = winrate vs baseline (Qwen3-30B-A3B judge). 50% = parity.

### Findings

1. **Dolci replay preserves English** (Track D): English Elo stays at 942-963 (baseline is 950), English arena-hard winrate ~55%. Without replay (Track A), English drops to 766-771 Elo / ~13% winrate. The source of the English data matters, the En/EU ratio doesn't.
2. **The D-track advantage is almost entirely English**: per-language Elo shows A vs D gap is ~190 points on English. On trained EU languages, they're within CIs.
3. **Scaling helps modestly**: E1 (90/10 at 491k) reaches the highest overall Elo (758). More EU data at scale (E2/E3) shows diminishing returns.
4. **More diverse data doesn't help** (Track B): 5× more data from wildchat/lmsys/oasst2 → similar Elo to Track A.
5. **Continued SFT itself causes forgetting** (Track C): C0 (100% English, no EU data at all) still drops English Elo to 791. The regression is not caused by EU data but by training on non-Dolci English.
6. **Transfer**: Romanian (held-out, Latin script) transfers well (Elo 700-890). Greek (held-out, different script) does not (540-690).

### Code

- Training configs: [`oellm/configs/`](https://github.com/ferreirafabio/open-instruct/tree/main/oellm/configs)
- Evaluation scripts: [`oellm/evaluations/benchmarks/`](https://github.com/ferreirafabio/open-instruct/tree/main/oellm/evaluations/benchmarks)

nodes.title: Add SFT to Torch Titan
nodes.description:
By adding SFT support, we can leverage TorchTitan’s 3D parallelism (FSDP2 /TP / CP) for instruction tuning, alignment task and reasoning tasks. Key implementation features on top of a general SFT loop would be-

a) Packed Sequence Loading with Masking: Implement a collator that packs variable-length instruction-response pairs into fixed blocks. Crucially, this must support label_mask to ensure loss is calculated only on assistant responses, not user prompts (as mentioned in this [Issue](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/Taskboard/issues/166)).

b) **Smart Batching & Auto-Accumulation**: Add a `BatchSizeConfig` utility that automatically calculates the optimal `micro_batch_size` and `gradient_accumulation_steps` based on detected hardware limits (e.g., H100 vs B200) to hit the target global batch size without OOM errors.

c) **Adaptive Context Parallelism**: Logic to dynamically switch CP strategies (e.g., from _ZigZag_ to _Ring/Llama3_ style) when packed datasets are detected, ensuring that attention masking correctly respects document boundaries across distributed ranks.

d) **Hybrid Checkpoint Recovery**: A robust loading mechanism that automatically detects context: it should strictly load weights-only when initializing from a pre-trained base model, but fully load optimizer states if resuming a crashed SFT run.

nodes.title: Add OBFD Packing to TRL/Torch Titan
nodes.description:
In [TRL](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/post-training), sequence packing currently relies on basic concatenation or simple "Best-Fit Bin Packing." These methods often lead to sub-optimal GPU utilization and complex attention masking requirements.

[OBFD](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.10830) (Overlapped Block-wise Fixed-size Dictionary) packing, as implemented in [OLMo-core](https://github.com/allenai/OLMo-core), offers a more deterministic and efficient way to pack variable-length sequences into fixed-size blocks. It would offer us-

- It minimizes padding tokens across distributed ranks, ensuring every training block is "full."
- It improves TFLOPS and training throughput by maximizing compute density.
- OLMo-3 utilizes this strategy to achieve significantly faster SFT speeds.

_Implementation caveats:_

_a) TRL: The target is to pre-pack and save the data as the SFT-Trainer accepts using the pre-tokenized data. But if we want to implement such packing for DPO-Trainer it would be difficult without creating a fork from TRL._ 

_b) TorchTitan- We can do it in a very similar way as pre-packing or also allow an option to dynamically do it within the SFT data loading script. In any case, this also is dependent upon implementing SFT on [TorchTitan](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/titan-oellm)._

nodes.title: test warmup effect on 50M model 6B
nodes.description:
In our Scaling Laws experiments, we set a fixed warmup duration (1000 iterations) across all runs, regardless of global batch size and token budget. Fixed warmup was chosen to be able to cool down at various token budgets and thus re-use previous runs and save compute. However, if global batch size and token budget differ, this means that a fixed warmup duration will represent a higher or lower fraction of training iterations. As we've calculated, the warmup duration will represent maximum 35% and minimum 0.25% of the total training iterations. 

Initial results with a long warmup fraction leads to higher loss. Here, we will sweep for the highest global batch size and the warmup fraction to verify if we obtain much lower loss or not. 

Model 50M, token budget 6B, global batch size 512, which results in 2861 iterations. Sweep over warmup fraction [1, 5, 10, 20] and learning rate [5.e-4, 1.e-3, 2.e-3, 4.e-3, 8.e-3]

nodes.title: Run vocabulary trimming experiment on trained models
Key Features decisions:Special Tokens (BOS), Whitespace, Reversibility, and Byte Fallback etc
nodes.description:
Beginning-of-Sentence (BOS) and End-of-Sentence (EOS) Tokens: A clear strategy is needed for how and when to insert BOS (e.g., [BOS] or <s>) and EOS (e.g., [EOS] or </s>) tokens. These markers are crucial for sequence demarcation, especially during training and inference, helping the model understand the start and end of a complete input unit.
Padding Token ([PAD]): Define the token used to ensure all sequences in a batch have the same length. This is essential for efficient batch processing on accelerated hardware.
Unknown/Out-of-Vocabulary Token ([UNK]): Establish the designated token for handling characters or subwords that are not present in the tokenizer's learned vocabulary. The behavior of the UNK token significantly impacts the model's ability to generalize to novel inputs.
Mask Token ([MASK]): If the tokenizer is intended for models utilizing masked language modeling (e.g., BERT), a dedicated mask token is required.
Whitespace Management:
Preservation vs. Stripping: Determine whether whitespace should be preserved as separate tokens/subwords or entirely stripped/collapsed. For many LLMs, whitespace is implicitly handled or represented by leading spaces in subword tokens (e.g., SentencePiece, BPE).
Normalization: Decide on a standard for normalizing different forms of whitespace (e.g., tabs, multiple spaces, non-breaking spaces) to a single canonical representation (e.g., a single ASCII space) before tokenization.
Reversibility (Decoding Accuracy):
Lossless Conversion: A critical feature for any production-grade tokenizer is the ability to losslessly convert a sequence of tokens back into the exact original text string, including all original spacing and punctuation. This ensures consistency and prevents unintended data corruption or manipulation between the tokenized and detokenized states.
Handling of Joiners: Ensure that the decoding process correctly handles the joining of subwords, particularly in models that rely on leading-space characters to denote the start of a new word.
Byte Fallback Mechanism:
Robustness for OOV: Implement a strategy to handle characters that cannot be represented even by the [UNK] token or high-frequency subwords. A byte-level fallback (e.g., using UTF-8 byte representations or individual character tokens) ensures that any input string, regardless of language or character set, can be tokenized. This is essential for achieving full language and character-set coverage and preventing errors on exotic or rare input characters.
Efficiency Trade-offs: While byte fallback is robust, it can lead to very long token sequences for highly out-of-vocabulary inputs, which has performance implications during training and inference. The design must balance robustness with efficiency..

[Multiblimp evaluation done by Sampo](https://mattermost.ufal.mff.cuni.cz/openeurollm/pl/digcii4q7jg8if7uiwg8r9kg7w) demonstrated that our 2B 4TT models are lower in language fluency compared to 2B 100BT monolingual reference models (both are trained on HPLT 2 cleaned).

Based on multi-staged training with uniform multilingual distribution presented by TildeOpen model we'll try to use equal distribution for decay training stage.

> The foundational model training involves 450,000 updates with a constant batch size of 4,718,592 tokens, using a constant learning rate followed by a cooldown phase across 2 trillion tokens. Training consists of three distinct data sampling phases. First, all languages are sampled uniformly to ensure equal representation. Second, languages are sampled according to their natural distribution to ensure that the model sees as much data from languages with larger speaker bases as possible. Finally, we return to uniform sampling across all languages. This three-phase approach ensures TildeOpen LLM develops balanced multilingual capabilities while maintaining strong performance across all target languages, particularly the underrepresented European languages.

We plan to run two experiments:
- use 2B 4TT model trained on 90% of English + code + math / 10% of multilingual data and apply uniform distribution for decay phase (starting from 765000 iteration)
- use 2B 4TT model trained on 50% of English + code + math / 50% of multilingual data and apply 90% English + code + math distribution for decay phase (starting from 765000 iteration)

nodes.title: Custom tokenizer for "flagship" models
nodes.description:
Based on experiments detailed [here](https://github.com/orgs/OpenEuroLLM/projects/6/views/6?pane=issue&itemId=114543717&issue=OpenEuroLLM%7CTaskboard%7C69), our recommendation is to use the gpt-oss tokenizer, with the additional note that when generating training data we should make sure that the BOS token is added to the start of documents (this does not currently seem to be happening with Megatron + HF tokenizer).

This recommendation is based in part on the following (no particular order):

- The gpt-oss tokenizer combines low fertility (good) for our target languages with a smaller vocabulary (also good) than Gemma 3 (200K vs. >260K)
- The tokenizer showed comparable performance to the Gemma 3 tokenizer in model training experiments
- The gpt-oss models (and hence the tokenizer, in our understanding) are under the permissive Apache 2 license and thus don't carry the licensing concerns that the Gemma 3 tokenizer that we have been using so far does.
- The gpt-oss tokenizer is used in a major OpenAI model release and thus unlikely to suffer from any serious errors in its design
- We were unfortunately not able to produce a custom OpenEuroLLM tokenizer that we would be confident in by this time.

Work on a custom tokenizer for the first "flagship" models due on Month 18 will continue, and we have tentatively given ourselves the following internal deadlines for these:

Flagship candidate tokenizers complete: Feb 2026 (Jonas+Felix?)
Flagship candidate tokenizers evaluated March 2026 (Fedor+?)

nodes.title: Post-training Llama-8B Models using different hyperparam configs on Tulu Datasets
nodes.description: Llama3.1-8B-Base models were **LoRA** fine-tuned on the Tulu-3-SFT dataset mix and code to check how different learning rates, warmup ratios, and LoRA ranks affect performance of fine-tuned models. The models were finetuned on **4 H100** GPUs for **one** epoch. # SFT Experimental Setting: Configurations mixed using: **Base Model:** Llama3.1-8B **Dataset:** Tulu-3-SFT-mix **LoRA Ranks** (LoRA alpha is set as Rank/4) = {64, 256, 1024} **Learning Rate (LR)** = {1e-6, 1e-5, 5e-5} **Warmup Ratio (WR)** = {0.001, 0.005, 0.01} And one with the Default hyperparameter setting from the Tulu3 codebase # Results The finetuned models were then tested using: **Benchmark:** Arena-Hard-v2.0 **No. of Instructions:** 750 **Baselines:** {Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Tulu-Llama3.1-8B} **Judge Model:** neuralmagic/Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-FP8 _It is important to keep in mind that the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Tulu-Llama3.1-8B had a more complex post-training pipeline (e.g. RLVR), whereas our models have only been fine-tuned using SFT on the Tulu3-SFT-Dataset for 1 epoch using the Tulu3 codebase_ ## Compared to Llama3.1-8B ## Compared to Llama3.1-8B-Instruct ## Compared to Tulu-Llama3.1-8B # Next Steps - [x] plot spearmanr across training iterations - to find the optimal rung sizes - [x] Plot validation loss curves for the finetuned models - [ ] Train models with same Rank, LR, and WarmupRatio but varying levels of LoRA alpha - is there an optimum LoRA alpha to rank relationship? - [x] Perform DPO on good, bad, and average performing SFT models to see if better performing SFT models also have better final model performance after RL? - [x] Perform SFT on some of the best checkpoints for one more epoch - [x] Compare performance of checkpoints from previous point with the Llama-Tulu-8B-SFT model (without RL) - [ ] change the dataset mixtures - possible combining with MF-BO

nodes.title: Implement anGPT/nGPT in torchtitan
nodes.description:
Implement anGPT in TorchTitan to test a few extensions and rework the scaling law we derived in https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22014

The goal is to provide an architecture for LLM pretraining that does not require learning rate warmup and regularization but increases convergence speed up to 40% while allowing larger batch sizes and therefore more efficient training. The scaling trend for the learning rate selection may be more stable.

nodes.title: Test mixing sources: finePDF (pdf CC), HPLT (web IA), Nemotron-CC (web CC)
nodes.description: Various source mixtures for dataset composition seems to further boost model training (preliminary evidence from finePDF study). We should test whether mixing IA, CC can create similar boost. Hypothesis to test is that diversity of sources in general increase model quality. Preliminary evidence from the plot: finePDF, FineWeb-edu, DCLM alone (or mix FineWeb-Edu/DCLM) have a decent level of performance, nothing exceptional. However mixing those creates strong boost above any single source. The question is: is it specific to pdf as data source for text, or is mixing various sources strongly beneficial in general? Eg, would mixing HPLT (as a different text source - Internet Archive) further boost dataset composition?

nodes.title: Multicluster setup for evaluations
nodes.description:
Implement the multi cluster setup described [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Q7JDxxj5vESJMuGIKNyEKn28z4pHUpmE8v9x8bHbuoo/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.g46l94ud1pxg).

In particular, we should support something like:

```bash
ssh lumi

# defines cluster specific env variables defined above, partition, HF_HOME, etc
source ~/clusterenv/cluster_env.sh  # sets up environment variables

srun --pty --nodes=1 --account=$slurm_default_account --partition $slurm_default_partition --time=60 /bin/bash

# function defined above that activates a project python venv to do eval
activate_lmeval  

# runs eval with the project shared venv 
lm_eval --model hf --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-160m,revision=step100000,dtype="float," \
    --tasks mmlu
```

where the code above runs on different system, we can start with Lumi and Juwels (Jureca), eg the command above should work for both lumi and jureca.

There a few steps that needs to be done:
* automatically detect cluster name given hostname 
* write a mechanism that allows to load environment variables of the detected system
* ship installed python environment in shared project folder for both that can run lm_eval
* test setup above work on two clusters

nodes.title: explore diffusion llm
nodes.description:
Diffusion language models (DLMs) have recently attracted significant attention across both academic and industry communities, with notable deployments including Google’s [Gemini Diffusion](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-diffusion/) and Inception Labs’ [Mercury](https://www.inceptionlabs.ai/introducing-mercury) and Meta's recent contribution, [EditFlows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09018). These models represent a fundamentally different approach to text generation, moving away from the traditional autoregressive models.

Diffusion language models work by corrupting sequences of coherent text to noisy versions of it and training a model to approximate the reverse corruption process (denoising). In contrast to autoregressive models, which generate tokens sequentially, diffusion language models leverage parallel decoding strategies, thereby presenting a promising approach to significantly reducing inference time (InceptionLabs reports a 10x speedup in decoding with Mercury). The number of generation steps is defined by a fixed denoising schedule, which can be considerably smaller than the length of the output sequence.

This paradigm presents several advantages: it enables **bidirectional context** modeling, **improves controllability** over generation (e.g., for editing or conditioning tasks), and demonstrates **competitive performance** with autoregressive counterparts across a range of benchmarks.

Earlier work, including the [D3PM framework](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2021/file/958c530554f78bcd8e97125b70e6973d-Paper.pdf) and [other studies](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05379), established the mathematical formulation for discrete diffusion models, defining both the corruption and denoising dynamics. Recent research has demonstrated the [scalability](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.18514) of diffusion language models up to 1B parameters. To date, the largest masked diffusion models are 7B [Dream](https://hkunlp.github.io/blog/2025/dream/) and 8B [LLaDa](https://ml-gsai.github.io/LLaDA-demo/). Recently, a [survey ](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.13759) on diffusion models for language models was released. 

In this work, we will explore whether diffusion language models are scalable and promising for the project:
- [ ] literature review
- [ ] run experiments with existing models (Dream and LLaDA)
- [ ] exploring scaling laws for diffusion language models.

Exclude contaminated samples from JudgeArena's win-rate tasks
nodes.description:
`collect --exclude_samples` now reports clean scores for JudgeArena's AlpacaEval, arena-hard and m-ArenaHard.

####  How it works

`<name>-annotations.csv` holds each battle's question and `results-<name>.json` the judge's preference in it, in the same order. With `swap_mode: both` (arena-hard), every question is judged twice: all direct battles first, then the reversed ones in the same order. 

Blocklist rows are matched to questions as follows (`sample-exclusion.yaml`):

- AlpacaEval by `instruction`, since JudgeArena numbers its questions by position.
- arena-hard and m-ArenaHard by `question_id`. arena-hard's uid is m-ArenaHard's `question_id`, and m-ArenaHard's ids are `<question_id>-<language>`, so one row excludes the question from arena-hard and from every m-ArenaHard language, including the `-EU` and all-language tasks.

`collect` then drops the excluded questions' battles, in every language and both orders, and recomputes:

- the plain win rate, (wins + ties / 2) / judged battles, with its counts
- AlpacaEval's raw win rate (the mean probability that the model wins)
- arena-hard's weighted win rate, in which a decisive verdict counts three times

AlpacaEval's length-controlled win rate is a regression over all battles and arena-hard's confidence intervals are bootstrapped, so both are left out with a warning. The ELO tasks fit ratings over all battles at once and get no clean rows; `collect` logs that once. 

####  How this was tested

- Unit tests with fake JudgeArena runs: each judging order, a question excluded in every language, unparsed verdicts, the reproduce check, the decisive weight, ELO and unsupported metrics refused, and the skipped cases.
- Every row of the AlpacaEval and m-ArenaHard blocklist files matches exactly one question of each mapped task, in every language, when the questions are loaded with JudgeArena's own loaders.
- On LUMI, 20-question runs of alpaca-eval, arena-hard-v0.1, arena-hard-v2.0 and m-arena-hard-v0.1-pl (SmolLM2-135M-Instruct judged by gemma-4-31b-it) all read correctly and reproduce their reported scores. Excluding a question drops one battle, or two in arena-hard.

- ~[ ] If this can change evaluation results (tasks, languages, shots, metrics, prompts, datasets, scoring), the line is under "Changed results"~ - this leaves existing scores unchanged, unless there was contamination

nodes.title: Score lighteval's corpus chrF, chrF++ and TER on every translation
nodes.description:
Fixes #169.

For chrF, chrF++ and TER, `lighteval` hands `sacrebleu` each sentence's references as a separate reference stream, which `sacrebleu` unintentionally only score the first translation (see huggingface/lighteval#1112). BLEU doesn't have this problem because `lighteval` already reshapes the references for it.

#### What this PR changes:

- `lighteval` loads `custom_lighteval_tasks/reasoning/reasoning.py` in every run, so the fix lives there. It gives chrF, chrF++ and TER the same reshape that `lighteval` already uses for BLEU.
- When the file loads, it runs a check and patches only the metrics that still score the first sentence alone. Once `lighteval` fixes this upstream, nothing gets patched and this code can be removed.
- When the fix is active, the job log shows a warning saying which metrics were patched.
- New tests check that chrF, chrF++ and TER now score the whole corpus, that BLEU is unchanged, and that nothing is patched if `lighteval` is already correct.
- `docs/TASKS.md` notes that passing your own file with `--lighteval_custom_tasks` replaces `reasoning.py`, so that file won't have the fix unless you copy it in.

`collect --exclude_samples` still leaves out clean chrF, chrF++ and TER scores. I haven't worked on that yet and will open a separate PR for it.

#### How this was tested:

I ran the tests with the LUMI container's `lighteval`, and they pass. I also re-scored a pythia-70m FLORES run from its saved outputs: it gives 13.42 without the fix and 8.09 with it, the same as `sacrebleu` gives used directly.

#### Checklist

- [x] Added a line to `CHANGELOG.md` under `## [Unreleased]` (not needed for CI, test or refactoring changes)
- [x] If this can change evaluation results (tasks, languages, shots, metrics, prompts, datasets, scoring), the line is under "Changed results"

nodes.title: Drop Latvian, Lithuanian, Maltese and Slovenian from belebele-eu-cf

```
AttributeError: Translation for 'answer' is needed for Language.LATVIAN
```

Every lighteval release so far is affected (huggingface/lighteval#1471). Until it's fixed, every `belebele-eu-cf` run produces four failed jobs, and `--check` lists them as missing.

This fixes #170.

#### Changes

- `belebele-eu-cf` runs 22 languages instead of 26, with a comment citing the relevant issue. `belebele-eu-5-shot` (lm-eval), which the `oellm-multilingual` groups use, still runs all four.
- The four cf tasks are removed from the Belebele entry in `sample-exclusion.yaml`, since every mapped task has to be in a group. agenttrove-0.0 flags no Belebele rows, so no clean scores change.
- The test that counts the group's tasks expects 22 instead of 26 now.

Asking for a dropped language explicitly now fails at schedule time with a clear message 
```
belebele-eu-cf[lvs_Latn]: "No tasks in task group 'belebele-eu-cf' match language(s) {lvs_Latn}")
```
instead of a failed job.

#### To Dos when the upstream `lighteval` issue is fixed

- set the test to 26 again

#### Testing

nodes.title: lighteval bug: FLORES chrF++ scores are wrong
nodes.description:
`lighteval` passes corpus chrF, chrF++ and TER references to `sacrebleu` in the wrong layout. `sacrebleu` then scores only the first translation of a task, against every sentence's reference. This is an open issue huggingface/lighteval#1112, with two unmerged fixes (huggingface/lighteval#1176, huggingface/lighteval#1234). It is still unfixed on lighteval `main`.

Affects every `lighteval` release so far (checked v0.5.0 to v0.13.0, and main at `b97a653`). Before v0.11.0, BLEU was affected too.

Effect on oellm:

- `flores-200-eu-to-eng` and `flores-200-eng-to-eu` report `chrf++`, so every FLORES score we have reported is likely wrong
- `collect --exclude_samples` recomputes chrF++ the same way `lighteval` does, so the clean FLORES scores would be wrong too
- The saved outputs are fine, so runs made with `--log_samples` can be rescored. Runs without saved details would have to be run again.

To do:

- [ ] Pick a fix: wait for huggingface/lighteval#1176 or huggingface/lighteval#1234 to be merged and rebuild the container, or patch lighteval's `CorpusLevelTranslationMetric` in our image.
- [ ] Rescore or re-run existing FLORES results, and add a line under "Changed results" in the CHANGELOG.
- [ ] Once `lighteval` is fixed, make `collect --exclude_samples` compute chrF++ the corrected way, so clean scores match.

nodes.title: Exclusion of samples from tasks not supported by lm-eval-harness
nodes.description:
This issue tracks what is still pending in terms of exclusion of contaminated samples from benchmarks.

#### Benchmarks that can't be excluded yet

- [ ] **No task in `lm-eval`, `lighteval` or `evalchemy`:** DS1000, MT-MBPP, GSM-Symbolic, SuperGPQA. Covering them would need new custom tasks. 
- [ ] **`evalchemy` benchmarks without per-question results:** HumanEval and HumanEval+ (lm-eval now covers these, but `evalchemy`'s runs in `reasoning` can't be filtered), LiveCodeBench, HLE, MultiPL-E (212 flagged rows, the most of any benchmark), MBPP+ and MMLU-Pro. Only MATH500 can be filtered, because evalchemy keeps every question and answer for it. The others need `evalchemy` to save per-question results (which we do not support as of now)
- [ ] **`JudgeArena`:** AlpacaEval, m-ArenaHard, m-ArenaHard v2 and v2.1.

#### Gaps in how exclusion works

- [ ] **A subject run on its own gets no clean row.** Benchmarks are mapped to groups (`mmlu`, `minerva_math`, `mmlu_redux_generative`), so `collect --exclude_samples` filters group runs only
- [ ] **Some scores are never recomputed:** bootstrapped standard errors, and lighteval's chrF, chrF++ and TER. `collect` leaves these out with a warning.

#### Known and accepted

The decontaminated run and `collect --exclude_samples` differ slightly for tasks that draw few-shot examples at random (GSM8K, BoolQ, MGSM). Skipping questions shifts the random draw. This is documented in the README, and no fix is planned as of Nov. 2026.

nodes.title: Investigate large CoQA generative F1 swings across Prelude checkpoints (MC accuracy stable)
nodes.description:
## Summary

The public Prelude checkpoint evaluation dataset shows unusually large checkpoint-to-checkpoint swings in **generative CoQA F1** for `prelude_anneal2t`, while the CoQA multiple-choice score and other generative QA benchmarks remain comparatively stable.

This is an **investigation request**, not a confirmed bug in `oellm-eval`. The underlying cause could be model output formatting, stopping/generation behavior, scoring, or genuine model changes.

## Evidence

Source: [OpenEuroLLM Prelude base evaluation scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openeurollm/prelude-base-eval-scores), `scores.parquet`. Filter: `model == "prelude_anneal2t"`, `task == "coqa_gen"`, `metric == "f1"`.

| Checkpoint step | CoQA generated F1 | CoQA MC accuracy | SQuAD generated F1 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1,092,000 | 0.320 | 0.856 | 0.901 |
| 1,094,400 | 0.745 | 0.861 | 0.905 |
| 1,096,800 | 0.507 | 0.847 | 0.899 |
| 1,099,200 | 0.733 | 0.848 | 0.895 |

Across the 81 available `prelude_anneal2t` checkpoints, the median absolute *adjacent-checkpoint* F1 change is:

| Task | Median absolute change |
| --- | ---: |
| `coqa_gen` | **0.0766** |
| `deu_coqa_gen` | 0.0264 |
| `drop_gen` | 0.0087 |
| `squad_gen` | 0.0048 |

The largest adjacent `coqa_gen` swing is **0.4244**. These are descriptive changes, not statistical significance tests.

## Configuration checks

For all 81 `coqa_gen` F1 entries:

- `n_samples`: **7,983** throughout.
- The serialized `task_config` is identical.
- `eval_config` is identical after excluding `model_name` (checkpoint path) and `total_eval_time_seconds`.
- Recorded evaluator version: `lm_eval 0.4.13.dev0`, git hash `45ab400`; model source `local-completions`.
- Generation config: `do_sample: false`, `temperature: 0.0`, `max_gen_toks: 50`, stops at `\n\n`, `Answer:`, or `Question:`.
- OpenEuroLLM's `task-groups.yaml` lists CoQA as 0-shot F1 with dataset `EleutherAI/coqa`.

This makes a changed benchmark configuration or changed sample count an unlikely explanation, but **does not** rule out inference nondeterminism or checkpoint-specific generation behavior.

## Suggested reproduction / diagnosis

1. Run the same `coqa` task with sample logging enabled (e.g. `--log_samples` in the evaluation harness), ideally on steps **1,092,000** and **1,094,400**, keeping evaluator/container/backend/settings identical.
2. Compare the same document IDs, prompt text, raw generated text, stop reasons (if available), normalized predictions, and per-sample F1.
3. Categorize errors: extra answer preambles, multi-line completions, premature stops, empty answers, answer normalization, genuinely wrong answers.
4. If possible, repeat one checkpoint to test deterministic generation through `local-completions`.
5. Compare the results to `coqa_mc` and `squad_gen` as controls.

**Question for maintainers:** Are per-sample logs or these two checkpoint endpoints accessible? The published `scores.parquet` exposes aggregate metrics and HPC result paths, but not generated answers, so I cannot independently confirm a root cause or a code fix yet.

Happy to help analyze anonymized/sample-level outputs or implement a focused regression test once the failure mode is identified.

nodes.title: PolyMath: 5-shot with boxed examples, out of multilingual-oellm-eu; fix scorer hang
nodes.description: PolyMath runs 0-shot, and base models score near 0 there: they rarely write an answer in `\boxed{}`, so almost nothing gets scored. This PR runs all four tiers 5-shot, leaves PolyMath out of `multilingual-oellm-eu`, and fixes a scorer hang that 5-shot makes likely. - Few-shot examples end in `\boxed{answer}`. PolyMath has no worked solutions, so they show only the answer. - `polymath_*_medium` draws its examples from low (`fewshot_split: low`). Low, high and top draw from their own tier, and lm-eval leaves out the scored item. - `multilingual-oellm-eu` runs no PolyMath tier (401 → 377 evals). The four `polymath-eu-*` groups stay, 5-shot. The PolyMath entries in `decontaminated-agenttrove-0.0` follow the new shots. - The scorer runs its sympy checks in a worker process that is killed and restarted on timeout, instead of in a thread it cannot stop. ## Results Mean of de, en, es, fr, it, pt over 10 checkpoints of `openeurollm/datamix-2b-80-20` (2B, steps 100k–950k) and `openeurollm/prelude` (9B, steps 100,800–953,312), 125 questions per language: | Setup | 2B | 9B | 9B, first → last 3 checkpoints | Kendall τ, 2B / 9B | |---|---:|---:|---|---| | medium, 0-shot (current) | 0.000 | 0.002 | 0.002 → 0.002 | – / −0.12 | | medium, 5-shot, examples from low | 0.018 | 0.027 | 0.026 → 0.034 | 0.18 / 0.41 | | medium, 5-shot, examples from medium | 0.022 | 0.032 | 0.032 → 0.032 | 0.05 / 0.20 | | low, 5-shot | 0.024 | 0.091 | 0.075 → 0.106 | 0.18 / 0.60 | | medium, always boxing 1 | 0.024 | 0.024 | | | - **Medium is at the floor.** 3 of its 125 questions have the answer 1 in every language, and about a quarter of the models' boxed medium answers are 1; on the 2B, 52 of 132 correct answers are those questions. Between checkpoints medium moves by about 0.01, 40% of its level. - **Low tracks training on the 9B only**, and reproduces the earlier figure (0.072 → 0.097 here, 0.070 → 0.103 before). It repeats MGSM questions that `mgsm-eu` and `global-mgsm-eu` already run in en/de/es/fr. - High and top, from the earlier runs at the last checkpoint: also at the floor, with the models boxing 1 on about a third of high's questions. So `multilingual-oellm-eu` runs none of them. Larger or instruction-tuned models can still run the `polymath-eu-*` groups. ### Low examples push medium toward integers Every low answer is an integer; 55 of medium's 125 are. On medium questions whose answer is not an integer, examples from low raise the share of boxed integers from 44% to 51% (2B) and 47% to 56% (9B). On the same questions they score 0.005 below examples from medium on both models (95% CI −0.008 to −0.002). Both sit at the floor, so this PR keeps low. ## Scorer hang One of the 80 audit runs (9B, step 199,200, medium) finished generating and then froze until the job's time limit, over 2 hours. `call_with_timeout` ran each sympy check in a daemon thread and abandoned it after 1 s. Abandoned threads keep running, and one evaluating a huge integer power inside `Expr.equals` holds the GIL in a single C call, so lm-eval never runs again. Replaying that run's 750 answers in one process froze with three abandoned threads alive. At 0-shot 3–12% of answers are boxed and checked; at 5-shot over 92%. The checks now go to a worker process that runs `polymath_eval.py` fresh (forking breaks latex2sympy2_extended, as noted in the file). On timeout the worker is killed and restarted (about 2.5 s), and the check returns False as before. - The frozen run now scores in 150 s. - Rescoring 8 other runs (6,000 answers) gives identical scores. - `tests/test_polymath_scorer.py` scores `\boxed{10^{10^{10}}}` as wrong within the timeout and keeps scoring; on the old scorer it hangs past pytest's own timeout. - End to end in the LUMI container, the frozen run again (9B, step 199,200, medium, 750 questions): lm-eval scores it in 77 s after generating, 14 correct, the same as scoring its outputs outside lm-eval with a hard per-check timeout. ## Audit setup LUMI container (lm-eval 0.4.13), this PR's task files at 5e8ef8d, greedy, batch size 32. Medium with examples from medium is an audit-only task with `fewshot_split: medium`. Code and per-sample outputs: `/scratch/project_465002530/users/haider/ML_Evals/audits/polymath_medium` on LUMI. Docs: [haideraltahan/mintlify-docs#1](https://github.com/haideraltahan/mintlify-docs/pull/1). ## To do - [ ] Drop the two WIP figure commits (b77b9ea, 8cae014); they are there only for this description. - [x] Docs: [haideraltahan/mintlify-docs#1](https://github.com/haideraltahan/mintlify-docs/pull/1), merged, so the site already describes this PR. - [x] Added a line to `CHANGELOG.md` under `## [Unreleased]` (not needed for CI, test or refactoring changes) - [x] If this can change evaluation results (tasks, languages, shots, metrics, prompts, datasets, scoring), the line is under "Changed results"

nodes.title: Report scores without contaminated samples
nodes.description:
Added two ways to evaluate on benchmarks while excluding the rows that were flagged during decontamination (but trained on anyway). 

I know this is a lot to review, but most of the diff is generated data. The actual code to review is at the end. 

--- 
#### 1. `collect --exclude_samples <dir>`

This is used to recompute the scores from a normal run's saved samples, while excluding the blocklisted (decontaminated) rows. `<dir>` holds one `<benchmark>.jsonl` per benchmark (e.g. agenttrove-0.0's `dropped/`)

Each affected task gets a second row in the CSV with `subset=clean` and `n_excluded` (this is the score that should be reported, because it is on the decontaminated set). The existing rows get `subset=full`.

- A row is excluded in every language **AND** in benchmarks holding (translated) copies of it (GSM8K in MGSM/Global-MGSM/PolyMath, X-CSQA in CommonsenseQA, FLORES-200 in SIB-200, WSC in English XWinograd). `oellm/resources/sample-exclusion.yaml` has a mapping for these. Translations that share no id are matched through alignment tables in `oellm/resources/sample-exclusion-alignments/`, which was built by using `scripts/build_sample_exclusion_alignments.py`.
- The saved samples must first reproduce the reported score, or `collect` stops with an error. A metric that can't be recomputed exactly (corpus F1, bootstrapped stderrs, lighteval's chrF/TER) is left out with a warning. A run without saved samples, or run with `--limit`, gets no clean rows and a warning.

---
#### 2. Task group `decontaminated-agenttrove-0.0`

This is an easy fix to run evals on Tudor's filtered dataset that was stored on LUMI (agenttrove-0.0). It runs the affected benchmarks on the FILTERED dataset (the dataset by Tudor that filtered out the contaminated samples).

The samples that are skipped are stored in the repo (`oellm/resources/decontaminated/agenttrove-0.0.json`, built by `scripts/build_decontaminated_samples.py`), so you don't need the pipeline's output to run the group. 

The results appear in `collect`'s CSV with `subset=decontaminated:agenttrove-0.0`. The group is not part of `all`.

---
#### How I tested it

- Lots of unit tests
- GPU test on a small pythia model

Runs that don't use these features are unchanged. I compared it against `main` (4330f3d) to make sure nothing broke:
- `schedule --dry_run`: `jobs.csv` was identical
- Job scripts: the same lm-eval and lighteval calls as before
- `collect` on 34 real result folders: identical output

---
### For the one reviewing this:

50K+ of the added lines are generated JSON (the alignment tables and the list of skipped questions). 

The actual code to review is in:
- `oellm/sample_exclusion.py`, `oellm/decontaminated.py`
- `oellm/main.py`, `oellm/task_groups.py`, `oellm/resources/template.sbatch`
- `oellm/resources/sample-exclusion.yaml`, `oellm/resources/task-groups.yaml`
- `scripts/build_sample_exclusion_alignments.py`, `scripts/build_decontaminated_samples.py`

---
Usage is documented in the README under "Scores without contaminated samples" and "Evaluating without contaminated samples".

Fixes #149.
- [x] Added a line to `CHANGELOG.md` under `## [Unreleased]` (not needed for CI, test or refactoring changes)
- ~[ ] If this can change evaluation results (tasks, languages, shots, metrics, prompts, datasets, scoring), the line is under "Changed results"~  (existing scores dont change, but benchmarks that had contamination should be re-run)

nodes.title: OpenSubtitles: 5-shot from a held-out movie, chrF as the metric
nodes.description: At 0-shot, `opensubtitles-eu-en-xx` and `opensubtitles-eu-xx-en` follow output format more than translation quality. The prompt ends with `Translation:\n` and `\n` is the first stop sequence, so a checkpoint that starts its answer with another newline returns an empty string. Without examples, small models also answer in English or copy the source. Both rates change from checkpoint to checkpoint, and the score moves with them. This PR: - runs both groups 5-shot with lm-eval's default sampler (random examples for each sentence, fixed seed) - takes the examples from one held-out movie (`27195590_17677860_1_6`, the smallest at 311 sentences), returned as a `fewshot` split and removed from the scored set (6,005 → 5,694 sentences per pair) - reports chrF instead of BLEU: over training, its gain relative to noise is 1.2–1.7× BLEU's **Audit:** `openeurollm/datamix-2b-80-20` and `openeurollm/prelude-checkpoints`, 10 checkpoints each, 8 prompt variants, de/el/fi/fr/lv/pl in both directions, 500 sentences per pair, 1,000 paired bootstrap resamples. chrF, mean of six languages, with 95% intervals. Light grey: current setup. Black: this PR. | Variant | Significant drops | Kendall τ | Empty or wrong-language English→X | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Instruction 0-shot (current) | 16 | 0.51 | 7–28% | | Instruction 0-shot, no final newline | 32 | 0.07 | 27–100% | | Instruction 1-shot | 0 | 0.81 | 6–10% | | **Instruction 5-shot (this PR)** | **0** | **0.84** | **6–8%** | | Plain 0-shot | 20 | 0.48 | 9–85% | | Plain 1-shot | 6 | 0.79 | 7–17% | | Plain 5-shot | 3 | 0.83 | 6–10% | | Plain 5-shot, fixed examples | 7 | 0.78 | 7–17% | A significant drop is a fall of the six-language mean between adjacent checkpoints in ≥95% of resamples, counted over 72 comparisons per variant (2 models × 2 directions × chrF and BLEU × 9 steps). Kendall τ is 1 when every later checkpoint scores higher. The language identifier itself misclassifies 6.5% of the references, so that is the floor for the last column. On Prelude English→X, the current setup's three significant drops (360k, 600k and 840k steps) fall on the three checkpoints where its empty outputs jump (11%, 8% and 12%). Empty or wrong-language English→X outputs per checkpoint. The dotted line is the language identifier's error on the references. ### The variants on one sentence English → German, "Who do we put in the shop window?" (reference: "Wen platzieren wir noch im Schaufenster?"), answered by Prelude's final checkpoint (`iter_0953312`). Prompts are written as Python strings so the newlines show. **Instruction 0-shot (current).** Output: empty. The checkpoint starts its answer with another newline, which stops generation. ```python "Translate the following sentence from English to German:\nWho do we put in the shop window?\nTranslation:\n" ``` **Instruction 0-shot, no final newline.** The obvious one-line fix. Output: empty again, because the model still puts its answer on a new line. 89–100% of datamix and 20–96% of Prelude English→X outputs come back empty. ```python "Translate the following sentence from English to German:\nWho do we put in the shop window?\nTranslation:" ``` **Instruction 1-shot and 5-shot (this PR uses 5).** The current prompt, preceded by 1 or 5 solved examples drawn at random for each sentence. The examples show the model where the answer goes and in which language. Output: `Wer stellen wir in das Schaufenster?` (1-shot), `Wer soll in das Schaufenster?` (5-shot). The 1-shot prompt: ```python "Translate the following sentence from English to German:\nWhere's our Jason?\nTranslation:\nWo ist unser Jason?\n\nTranslate the following sentence from English to German:\nWho do we put in the shop window?\nTranslation:\n" ``` **Plain 0-shot.** Language names only, answer after a space. Output: `Wer kommt in den Schaufenster?`. On datamix, 44–85% of English→X outputs are in the wrong language, mostly English. ```python "English: Who do we put in the shop window?\nGerman:" ``` **Plain 1-shot, 5-shot, and 5-shot with fixed examples.** The plain prompt with random examples, or with the same first five examples for every sentence (`sampler: first_n`). Output: `Wen stellen wir in das Schaufenster?` for all three. Plain 5-shot scores within noise of instruction 5-shot but drops significantly 3 times. Fixed examples drop 7 times, and datamix English→X collapses at 250k steps (31.2 → 25.4 chrF). The 1-shot prompt: ```python "English: Where's our Jason?\nGerman: Wo ist unser Jason?\n\nEnglish: Who do we put in the shop window?\nGerman:" ``` ### Notes - **Breaks comparability:** OpenSubtitles scores move to a different level (Prelude's final checkpoint, English→X chrF on the audit languages: 37.9 → 46.1), the group metric changes, and one movie leaves the scored set. - **Cost:** 5-shot took 25–30% more GPU time per checkpoint than 0-shot. - **Held-out movie:** the audit drew its examples from 32 random sentences of the same movies as the scored set. This PR holds out a whole movie so no example shares a scene with a scored sentence. - **Tested:** `pytest tests` passes. In the LUMI container, Prelude's final checkpoint on 50 sentences of `en_to_de` and `el_to_en`: every prompt has 5 examples from the held-out movie, no output is empty, chrF 53.9 and 50.2. - Audit code and per-sample outputs are in `/scratch/project_465002530/users/haider/ML_Evals/audits/opensubtitles_signal` on LUMI.

nodes.title: Set n_shots: [10] for multilingual HellaSwag to align with original
nodes.description: We currently run the original HellaSwag by default with `n_shots: [10]` in the [open-sci-0.01](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/oellm-eval/blob/main/oellm/resources/task-groups.yaml#L42) task group and `n_shots: [0, 10]` in the [dclm-core-22](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/oellm-eval/blob/main/oellm/resources/task-groups.yaml#L333) task group, but run the multilingual HellaSwag ([hellaswag-eu](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/oellm-eval/blob/main/oellm/resources/task-groups.yaml#L457) group) with `n_shots: [0]`. The fewshot settings used for HellaSwag in related work vary, for example * [Apertus](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.14233#page=44): 0-shot * [Olmo 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.13961#page=99): 5-shot * [DeepSeek V3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.19437#page=25): 10-shot Evaluation results for openeurollm/datamix-2b-80-20 checkpoints with Gemma 4 for reference, original HellaSwag, `acc_norm`: Same for multilingual HellaSwag, averaged over hellaswag_ca, hellaswag_da, hellaswag_de, hellaswag_es, hellaswag_eu, hellaswag_fr, hellaswag_hr, hellaswag_hu, hellaswag_it, hellaswag_nl, hellaswag_pt, hellaswag_ro, hellaswag_sk, hellaswag_sr, hellaswag_sv, hellaswag_uk: We see basically the same pattern, with 10-shot eval providing a small-to-moderate but consistent improvement over 0-shot. While the difference isn't large, I see no reason to use different n_shot settings for the original and multilingual versions. This PR aligns the two by setting `n_shots: [10]` for multilingual HellaSwag; a (costlier) alternative would be to match DCLM-core and use `n_shots: [0, 10]`.

nodes.title: Pass --debug to evalchemy when --limit is set
nodes.description:
Fixes #154.

evalchemy forwards `--limit` only to lm-eval tasks. Its own benchmarks, which are all seven evalchemy tasks in `reasoning` (MATH500, GPQADiamond, LiveCodeBench, HumanEval, AIME24, AIME25, AMC23), read every question and shrink only under `--debug`. A `--limit` smoke test of `reasoning` therefore ran them in full, while the results file still recorded the limit.

The template now passes `--debug` along with `--limit` to evalchemy. In the fork we install (Ali-Elganzory/evalchemy @ 54ac976), `--debug` keeps the first 2 questions of each of these benchmarks (10 for LiveCodeBench) and otherwise only skips evalchemy's database upload, which we don't use. `--limit` stays so lm-eval tasks run through evalchemy still get it. Since the subset size is fixed whatever N is, `schedule` logs a warning when a limited run includes evalchemy tasks, and the `limit` docstring says so.

The new test renders a `--limit 2` run of MATH500 and checks for `--debug` and the warning. It fails on main.

nodes.title: `--limit` is ignored for evalchemy benchmarks
nodes.description:
### oellm-eval version

oellm-eval 0.4.0b1 (editable install) | python 3.12.15 | datasets 5.1.0 | huggingface_hub 2.3.0 
Output of `git rev-parse --short HEAD: b073b4b` evalchemy: Ali-Elganzory/evalchemy @ 54ac976

### Cluster

LUMI

### Runtime

Own environment (--venv_path)

### Command

```shell
oellm-eval schedule --models <model> --task_groups reasoning --limit 2 --venv_path <evalchemy-venv>

To reproduce it, I ran the evalchemy call that template.sbatch makes (line 287–294):


source env.sh
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 HF_DATASETS_OFFLINE=1
cd evalchemy
python -m eval.eval \
    --model hf \
    --tasks MATH500 \
    --model_args "trust_remote_code=True,pretrained=HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct,device=cpu" \
    --batch_size 8 \
    --output_path "$OUT" \
    --limit 2
```

### What happened, and what did you expect?

**Expected:** 
MATH500 evaluated on 2 questions.

**Happened:** 
All 500 questions were evaluated. The results file still has `config.limit = 2.0` so it looks like a limited run.

**Reason:** 
In evalchemy's `eval/eval.py`, `args.limit` is passed only to `lm-eval` tasks (line 241). None of evalchemy's own benchmarks (MATH500, GPQADiamond, LiveCodeBench, HumanEval, AIME24/25, AMC23) accept a limit. It expects `--debug` flag to run a short pre-defined subset instead. 

`oellm-eval` passes `--limit` to the `evalchemy` suite (`template.sbatch line 294`), which can give the impression that the user is only running evals on a limited set of questions. This issue exists upstream in `mlfoundations/evalchemy`, so I have a couple of suggestions for a fix in `oellm-eval` suggested below.

**Impact:** 
A `--limit` smoke test of `reasoning` silently runs the full benchmarks

**Possible fixes:**
- Map `--limit` to evalchemy's `--debug` for smoke-tests
- Warn or refuse when `--limit` is used with evalchemy tasks

### Logs

```text
INFO [eval.py:381] Selected Tasks: ['MATH500']
INFO [eval.py:188] Benchmark tasks to evaluate: ['MATH500']
INFO [eval_instruct.py:139] Loaded 500 questions from eval/chat_benchmarks/MATH500/data/math500.jsonl
Running generate_until requests:   0%|          | 0/500 [00:00<?, ?it/s]
...
INFO [eval.py:635] Eval arugments: hf (trust_remote_code=True,pretrained=HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct,device=cpu), gen_kwargs: (None), limit: 2.0, num_fewshot: None, annotator_model: auto, batch_size: 8 (8)
===== exit status: 0 =====
===== results_2026-10-28T15-39-14.281730.json: config.limit=2.0, MATH500 questions scored=500 =====
```

nodes.title: Should xcopa-eu run 5-shot with lm-eval's xcopa tasks?
nodes.description: `xcopa-eu` runs lighteval's `xcopa:{lang}` at 0 shots (#66). On `openeurollm/datamix-2b-80-20` it scores close to chance (0.549 over et, it and tr; Estonian 0.52 at the last checkpoint). Raising `n_shots` alone won't work: lighteval looks for few-shot examples in a train split, and XCOPA only has validation (100 items per language) and test (500). ## Proposal Run lm-eval's bundled `xcopa_{lang}` at 5 shots, scored with `acc`: ```yaml xcopa-eu: description: "XCOPA commonsense causal reasoning (5-shot, acc) for EU languages." suite: lm-eval-harness metric: acc n_shots: [5] dataset: cambridgeltl/xcopa valid_langs: [et, it, tr] tasks: - task: "xcopa_{lang}" subset: "{lang}" ``` lm-eval takes the examples from validation and scores test, and the two splits share no premises. The prompt is the one lm-eval's `copa` uses for English: the premise without its period, "because" or "therefore" in the item's language, then the choice. ## Results et, it and tr on 10 checkpoints each of `openeurollm/datamix-2b-80-20` (2B) and `openeurollm/prelude` (9B, before cooldown). Mean accuracy: | Setup | 2B | 9B | |---|---|---| | lighteval, 0-shot (current) | 0.549 | 0.616 | | COPA prompt, 0-shot | 0.586 | 0.648 | | COPA prompt, 5-shot (proposed) | 0.615 | 0.725 | | COPA prompt, 10-shot | 0.622 | 0.735 | 5 and 10 shots are within 0.01, rise about the same over training and put the 9B 0.11 above the 2B at every checkpoint (0.067 with the current setup). 10 shots are slightly steadier on the 9B. OLMES also uses 5. ## Questions 1. 5 shots, or 10 like `sib200-eu` and `xcsqa-eu`? 2. Should English `copa` (0 shots now) use the same number of shots?

nodes.title: Add bits-per-byte (BPB) evaluation for small models
nodes.description:
Accuracy on downstream tasks sits at chance for very small models, so it cannot tell them apart. This blocks evaluating the many small models. Bits-per-byte (BPB) can still separate them, since it is tokenizer-agnostic and changes smoothly as a model assigns more probability to the right text.

This PR adds three task groups, plus a template for BPB on your own text. All of them report `bits_per_byte` (**lower is better**) 

| Group | What it scores | Shots |
|---|---|---|
| `bpb-corpus` | Held-out text: lm-eval's built-in `wikitext` (WikiText-2) | 0 |
| `bpb-flores-eu` | FLORES-200 `devtest` in the 36 OpenEuroLLM target languages, with each source article's sentences joined into one document | 0 |
| `bpb-mc-en` | Gold-answer BPB: only the correct answer's text on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, Social IQa and Winogrande | 5 |

### How it works
- **`bpb-corpus`** is configuration only. lm-eval already computes `bits_per_byte` for `wikitext`.
- **`bpb-flores-eu`** uses new custom `loglikelihood_rolling` tasks in `custom_lm_eval_tasks/flores_bpb/`.
- **`bpb-mc-en`** uses a new task class, `BPBTask`, in `custom_lm_eval_tasks/bpb_mc/bpb_task.py`. lm-eval computes no BPB for multiple-choice tasks.
  - Each `*_bpb` task wraps an existing lm-eval task by name, set with `base_task:` in a short YAML. It reuses that task's prompts and data, and reports only `bits_per_byte`.
  - Per question, it scores the correct answer's log-likelihood over the UTF-8 bytes of exactly what lm-eval scored: the target delimiter plus the answer. Winogrande-style tasks, where the choices are in the context, are handled.
  - The wrapped task's config is looked up at run time, because `include:` only takes file paths and the built-in task files live in different places in the venv and the container. The wrapped task's name and version are recorded in the results metadata.
- **BPB on your own text:** `custom_lm_eval_tasks/corpus_bpb/_corpus_bpb_template` is a commented template for local JSONL, Parquet or CSV files or a Hugging Face dataset. Users copy it into their own folder, fill in three lines, and run it with `--tasks <name> --n_shot 0 --lm_eval_include_path <folder>`. See the new "Bits-per-byte on your own text" section in `docs/TASKS.md`.
- **No changes** to scheduling, the sbatch template or `collect`. The new tasks have distinct names, so `primary_metric_map()` picks up `bits_per_byte` from `task-groups.yaml`.

### Things to be aware of
- **`facebook/flores` is gated.** The HF token used for the pre-download needs access to it.
- **`bpb-mc-en` needs lm-eval >= 0.4.12.** 
- **Only cloze-style tasks are wrapped.** CommonsenseQA and MMLU are left out because lm-eval scores them as letters ("A", "B", ...). For MMLU the cloze variant, `mmlu_continuation`, could be wrapped in a follow-up.
- **Own-text template:** `--lm_eval_include_path` replaces the bundled custom tasks for that run, so a user's own corpus should be scheduled in a run of its own. The data must be inside the task folder, which is mounted into the container, or be mounted separately.

### How this was tested
- **Unit tests:**
  - Task-group expansion, the dataset pre-download specs, and the task files matching their groups.
  - FLORES document joining.
  - `BPBTask` gold handling: index, answer text, several golds, NumPy integers, invalid golds and partial evaluation.
  - That collection keeps only `bits_per_byte`.
  - That the filled-in template loads a local file in lm-eval.
- **lm-eval versions:** the `BPBTask` and template tests pass on both lm-eval 0.4.12 and 0.4.13.
- **Independent checks:**
  - `arc_easy_bpb` matches gold-answer BPB recomputed from lm-eval `--log_samples` output to 15 digits.
  - All seven `*_bpb` tasks match the same recomputation at 5-shot. I checked Winogrande by hand against the dataset's `answer` field.
  - FLORES BPB matches an independent transformers computation exactly (in float32).
  - The own-text template, run on FLORES German exported to JSONL, reproduces `flores_bpb_deu_Latn` to all 16 digits.
- **On LUMI (pythia-70m):**
  - A SLURM job array over 16 FLORES languages completed.
  - `collect` returned all results, including all 7 `bpb-mc-en` tasks.
  - A dry run of `bpb-mc-en` pre-downloaded all datasets.

Fixes #117 

- [x] Added a line to `CHANGELOG.md` under `## [Unreleased]` (not needed for CI, test or refactoring changes)
- ~[ ] If this can change evaluation results (tasks, languages, shots, metrics, prompts, datasets, scoring), the line is under "Changed results"~
  - Not applicable: this adds new task groups and changes no existing task's results.

nodes.description:
This PR handles replacement of the current CSV format in the files generated by `schedule` (e.g. jobs.csv) and `collect` (results files).

This should remove the issues with processing and properly escaping commas, especially outside of Python (template.sbatch), simplifying the current codebase.
